Interpretation: General β-glucosidases (EC 3.2.1.21) are detected and may contribute to esculin hydrolysis, although their substrate specificity cannot be established from KO annotation alone.
References: James et al. (1997); Yang et al. (1995); Deflandre et al. (2022).

Interpretation: Neither of the evaluated β-glucosidase KO markers (K05349 or K05350) is detected.
References: James et al. (1997); Deflandre et al. (2022).

Interpretation: Beta-glucoside PTS components and a phospho-beta-glucosidase are detected, supporting the transport and subsequent hydrolysis of phosphorylated arbutin.
References: Zangoui et al. (2015); UniProtKB P17411; Weber et al. (1998, 2000).

Interpretation: Candidate enzymes for arbutin hydrolysis are detected, but the transport and processing criteria established for the Probable classification are not fulfilled.
References: Deflandre et al. (2022); Zangoui et al. (2015).

Interpretation: Beta-glucoside-related PTS components are detected, but none of the evaluated candidate enzymes required to support arbutin hydrolysis are identified.
References: Deflandre et al. (2022); Zangoui et al. (2015).

Interpretation: The candidate enzymes evaluated for the hydrolysis of arbutin are not detected.
References: Zangoui et al. (2015); Weber et al. (1998, 2000).

Interpretation: An acetate/butyrate-CoA ligase (K01913) or the combination of butyrate kinase (K00929) and phosphate butyryltransferase (K00634) is detected. These enzymes are compatible with the activation of butanoate to butyryl-CoA, suggesting the potential to use butanoate as a substrate.
References: KEGG bacc00650; Louis & Flint (2014).

Interpretation: Enzymes associated with acyl-CoA metabolism and β-oxidation are detected, but the genomic markers evaluated for direct butanoate activation are absent. Therefore, the genomic evidence is insufficient to confirm the potential to use butanoate as a substrate.
References: KEGG bacc00650; Louis & Flint (2014).

Interpretation: None of the genomic markers evaluated for butanoate activation or metabolism are detected.
References: KEGG bacc00650; Louis & Flint (2014).

Interpretation: A glutamyl endopeptidase with experimentally demonstrated hydrolytic activity against α-casein and β-casein is detected.
References: Kalyankar et al. (2013a, 2013b).

Interpretation: An extracellular neutral metalloprotease potentially involved in protein degradation is detected, although its specific activity against casein has not been demonstrated.
References: MEROPS M04.012; Harwood & Kikuchi (2022).

Interpretation: None of the candidate proteases evaluated for casein degradation are detected.
References: MEROPS M04.012; Song et al. (2023).

Interpretation: A complete cellobiose ABC transport system accompanied by a β-glucosidase or cellobiose phosphorylase is detected, or a complete cellobiose-specific PTS system accompanied by a 6-phospho-β-glucosidase is detected. These combinations support the potential uptake and intracellular processing of cellobiose.

Partial components of a cellobiose transport system or a broader β-glucoside PTS system are detected, together with enzymes potentially involved in cellobiose processing. However, the genomic evidence does not meet the criteria for a complete and specific transport and processing system.
Individual transport or processing markers are detected, but the available genomic evidence does not establish a compatible combination of cellobiose uptake and intracellular processing.
None of the genomic markers evaluated for cellobiose transport or intracellular processing are detected.

The three citrate lyase subunits, the associated citrate lyase ligase and the holo-ACP synthase required for enzyme maturation are detected. This combination supports the potential for intracellular citrate cleavage into acetate and oxaloacetate.
A citrate transport system or individual components associated with citrate lyase are detected, but the genomic evidence does not establish a complete citrate uptake and degradation system.
Components of the ferric citrate transport system are detected, suggesting a potential role in iron acquisition rather than citrate utilization as a carbon source.
None of the genomic markers evaluated for citrate transport, citrate lyase activity or ferric citrate uptake are detected.

A complete fructose utilization route is detected, involving fructokinase-mediated phosphorylation, a fructose-specific PTS system, or an ABC transport system, together with the enzymes required for subsequent carbohydrate metabolism.
References: Kornberg (2001); KEGG ko00051; KEGG K10552–K10554.

Interpretation: A complete or partially supported fructose uptake and phosphorylation mechanism is detected, but the genomic evidence does not establish all the downstream steps required for complete catabolism.
References: Kornberg (2001); KEGG ko00051.

Interpretation: Individual enzymes or transport components associated with fructose metabolism are detected, but the available genomic evidence is insufficient to establish a coherent fructose uptake and phosphorylation mechanism.
References: KEGG ko00051; KEGG K10552–K10554.

Interpretation: None of the genomic markers evaluated for fructose transport, phosphorylation or subsequent metabolism are detected.
References: KEGG ko00051.

Interpretation: A complete Leloir pathway or an alternative galactonate degradation pathway initiated by D-galactose oxidation is detected, supporting the potential to metabolize D-galactose and channel its carbon into central metabolism.
References: KEGG M00632; KEGG M00552; KEGG ko00052.

Interpretation: Partial components of the Leloir pathway or the alternative galactonate degradation pathway are detected, suggesting potential D-galactose metabolism, although the genomic criteria for a complete route are not fulfilled.
References: KEGG M00632; KEGG M00552; KEGG ko00052; Costantini et al. (2021).

Interpretation: Individual enzymes associated with the Leloir or galactonate degradation pathways are detected, but the available genomic evidence is insufficient to establish a complete or sufficiently supported route for D-galactose utilization.
References: KEGG M00632; KEGG M00552; KEGG ko00052.

Interpretation: None of the genomic markers evaluated for the Leloir or galactonate degradation pathways are detected.
References: KEGG M00632; KEGG M00552; KEGG ko00052.

Interpretation: A complete bacterial galacturonate degradation pathway is detected, either through the canonical isomerase pathway (UxaC–UxaB–UxaA) or through the alternative UxaE–UxuB–UxuA route, together with the downstream enzymes required for conversion of KDG into central metabolic intermediates.
References: KEGG M00631; KEGG ko00040; Kuivanen et al. (2019).

Interpretation: Partial components of the canonical isomerase pathway or the alternative UxaE-dependent route are detected, suggesting potential D-galacturonate catabolism, although the genomic evidence does not establish a complete pathway.
References: KEGG M00631; KEGG ko00040; Kuivanen et al. (2019).

Interpretation: Individual enzymes associated with the canonical or alternative galacturonate degradation pathways are detected, but the available genomic evidence is insufficient to establish a coherent catabolic route.
References: KEGG M00631; KEGG ko00040; Kuivanen et al. (2019).

Interpretation: None of the genomic markers evaluated for the canonical or alternative D-galacturonate degradation pathways are detected.
References: KEGG M00631; KEGG ko00040.

Interpretation: A gluconokinase capable of phosphorylating D-gluconate is detected together with enzymes supporting its subsequent metabolism through either the Entner–Doudoroff pathway or the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway.
References: KEGG K00851, K25031, K01690, K01625, K00033; KEGG ko00030; Mandrand-Berthelot et al. (2004).

Interpretation: A gluconokinase is detected without sufficient evidence of downstream catabolism, or the alpha and gamma subunits of gluconate 2-dehydrogenase are detected, suggesting a potential alternative oxidative route. However, the completeness of the oxidative enzyme complex and subsequent metabolism are not established.
References: KEGG K00851, K25031, K06150–K06152; KEGG R01741; Mandrand-Berthelot et al. (2004).

Interpretation: Individual enzymes associated with central carbohydrate metabolism or the oxidative conversion of gluconate and 2-ketogluconate are detected, but the genomic evidence does not establish a sufficiently supported route for D-gluconate utilization.
References: KEGG ko00030; KEGG K00874; KEGG K00065; Mandrand-Berthelot et al. (2004).

Interpretation: None of the genomic markers evaluated for D-gluconate phosphorylation, oxidative conversion or subsequent metabolism are detected.
References: KEGG ko00030; KEGG R01741; Mandrand-Berthelot et al. (2004).

Interpretation: A glucose phosphorylation or glucose-specific PTS uptake mechanism is detected together with enzymes supporting subsequent metabolism through the EMP or Entner–Doudoroff pathways. Alternatively, glucose oxidation to gluconate, followed by gluconate phosphorylation and downstream metabolism, is detected.
References: Del Castillo et al. (2007); Nikel et al. (2015); Wolfe (2015); KEGG map00010 and map00030.

Interpretation: Markers of glucose phosphorylation, PTS-mediated uptake or peripheral glucose oxidation are detected, but the available genomic evidence does not establish a complete route connecting glucose entry with downstream catabolism.
References: Del Castillo et al. (2007); Wolfe (2015); KEGG map00010 and map00030.

Interpretation: Enzymes associated with central carbohydrate metabolism, gluconate processing or downstream glucose catabolism are detected, but no specific markers of glucose uptake or initial phosphorylation are identified.
References: Wolfe (2015); KEGG map00010 and map00030.

Interpretation: None of the genomic markers evaluated for glucose uptake, phosphorylation, peripheral oxidation or subsequent catabolism are detected.
References: KEGG map00010; KEGG map00030.

Interpretation: Detection of the mannitol-specific PTS component(s) together with mannitol-1-phosphate 5-dehydrogenase, supporting PTS-mediated uptake and phosphorylation of D-mannitol followed by conversion of mannitol-1-phosphate into D-fructose-6-phosphate.
References: KEGG pathway kpe00051; IUBMB EC 1.1.1.17; Boulanger et al. (2021)

Interpretation: Detection of partial components of the mannitol-specific PTS together with the downstream dehydrogenase, or a putative polyol transport permease together with an alternative mannitol dehydrogenase, suggesting a potential but incompletely supported route for D-mannitol utilization.
References: Mayer and Boos (2005); Boulanger et al. (2021); KEGG KO K10228 and K00045

Interpretation: Detection of an isolated putative polyol transport permease or an alternative mannitol dehydrogenase, without sufficient evidence for coordinated uptake and catabolism.
References: KEGG KO K10228 and K00045

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with mannitol transport or metabolism are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize D-mannitol.
References: KEGG KO; IUBMB EC 1.1.1.17

Interpretation: Detection of the mannose-specific PTS, either as a fused component or as separate components, together with mannose-6-phosphate isomerase (ManA), supporting PTS-mediated uptake and phosphorylation of D-mannose followed by conversion of mannose-6-phosphate into D-fructose-6-phosphate.
References: KEGG ko00051; KEGG K01809; Boulanger et al. (2021).

Interpretation: Detection of partial components of the mannose-specific PTS together with an enzyme potentially capable of converting mannose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate, suggesting a potential but incompletely supported route for D-mannose utilization.
References: KEGG ko00051; KEGG K01809; KEGG K16011; Boulanger et al. (2021).

Interpretation: Detection of isolated enzymes associated with mannose metabolism, GDP-mannose biosynthesis or mannan degradation, without sufficient evidence for coordinated uptake and catabolism of D-mannose.
References: KEGG ko00051; KEGG K01809; KEGG K16011; KEGG K01840; KEGG K00971; KEGG K01192.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with D-mannose transport, metabolism or related pathways are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize D-mannose.
References: KEGG ko00051; KEGG send00051; Boulanger et al. (2021).

Interpretation: Detection of the complete RbsABC high-affinity ABC transporter together with ribokinase (RbsK), supporting D-ribose uptake and its phosphorylation to D-ribose-5-phosphate.
References: Lopilato et al. (1984); Iida et al. (1984); IUBMB EC 7.5.2.7; KEGG K00852.

Interpretation: Detection of ribokinase together with one or two components of the RbsABC transporter, suggesting potential D-ribose uptake and phosphorylation, although a complete high-affinity transport system is not identified.
References: Lopilato et al. (1984); Iida et al. (1984); Clifton et al. (2015).

Interpretation: Detection of isolated markers associated with D-ribose transport, phosphorylation or interconversion between its cyclic forms, without sufficient evidence for a coordinated uptake and catabolic system.
References: Lopilato et al. (1984); Iida et al. (1984); KEGG K06726; Clifton et al. (2015).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with D-ribose transport or metabolism are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize D-ribose, since alternative low-affinity transport systems may occur.
References: Lopilato et al. (1984); Iida et al. (1984).

Interpretation: Detection of the complete glucitol/sorbitol-specific PTS together with sorbitol-6-phosphate 2-dehydrogenase (SrlD), supporting PTS-mediated uptake and phosphorylation of D-sorbitol followed by conversion of sorbitol-6-phosphate into D-fructose-6-phosphate.
References: KEGG ko00051; IUBMB EC 1.1.1.140; UniProt P05707; PathBank PW002022.

Interpretation: Detection of the complete sorbitol-specific PTS without SrlD, or both subunits of the alternative acceptor-dependent D-sorbitol/glycerol dehydrogenase, suggesting potential D-sorbitol utilization through an incompletely supported or alternative route.
References: Pérez-Ramos et al. (2017); KEGG K08261 and K28751.

Interpretation: Detection of isolated components of the sorbitol-specific PTS or the alternative SldAB dehydrogenase, without sufficient evidence for a complete transport and metabolic system.
References: KEGG ko00051; KEGG K08261 and K28751; Pérez-Ramos et al. (2017).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with D-sorbitol transport or metabolism are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize D-sorbitol, as alternative pathways may occur.
References: KEGG ko00051; PathBank PW002022.

Interpretation: Detection of xylose isomerase (XylA) together with xylulokinase (XylB), supporting the classical conversion of D-xylose into D-xylulose, followed by phosphorylation to D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which can enter the pentose phosphate pathway.
References: Liu et al. (2015); Zhao et al. (2020); KEGG ko00040.

Interpretation: Detection of enzymes supporting the oxidative conversion of D-xylose into D-xylonate, followed by its dehydration to 2-keto-3-deoxy-D-xylonate. This suggests a potential alternative route, although the complete downstream pathway is not necessarily present.
References: Zhao et al. (2020); KEGG ko00040.

Interpretation: Detection of isolated markers associated with D-xylose transport, classical or oxidative catabolism, or the reductive pathway, without sufficient evidence for a complete uptake and utilization route.
References: Zhao et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2015); KEGG ko00040.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with D-xylose transport or metabolism are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize D-xylose, as alternative transport systems or metabolic pathways may occur.
References: Zhao et al. (2020); KEGG ko00040.

Interpretation: Detection of neutral peptidase B (NprB), an extracellular metalloprotease candidate that may contribute to gelatin hydrolysis, although its substrate specificity has not been established at the KO level.
References: KEGG BRITE; KEGG K08777.

Interpretation: Detection of isolated proteases associated with extracellular protein degradation, including glutamyl endopeptidase, generic serine protease, microbial collagenase, bacillolysin or aureolysin, without sufficient evidence to establish specific gelatinolytic activity.
References: Rice et al. (2001); IUBMB EC 3.4.24.3; KEGG BRITE; BRENDA EC 3.4.21.19.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated protease markers are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to hydrolyse gelatin, as divergent or unannotated extracellular proteases may be present.
References: KEGG BRITE; ASM Gelatin Hydrolysis Test Protocol.

Interpretation: Detection of glutarate dioxygenase (CsiD) together with L-2-hydroxyglutarate oxidase (LhgO), supporting the CsiD/LhgO pathway. CsiD converts glutarate into L-2-hydroxyglutarate, which is subsequently oxidized by LhgO to 2-oxoglutarate. The latter is regenerated and reused by CsiD, resulting in succinate and CO₂ production.
References: KEGG M00957; KEGG ko00310; Zhang et al. (2018); IUBMB EC 1.14.11.64.

Interpretation: Detection of glutaryl-CoA transferase together with glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, supporting glutarate activation to glutaryl-CoA and its subsequent oxidation to glutaconyl-CoA. This suggests a potential alternative route, although downstream conversion to acetyl-CoA is not confirmed.
References: KEGG M00957; KEGG ko00310; Folch (2021); Buckel and Thauer (2013).

Interpretation: Detection of isolated markers associated with the CsiD/LhgO pathway or glutaryl-CoA-dependent degradation, without sufficient evidence to establish either complete pathway.
References: KEGG M00957; Zhang et al. (2018).

Interpretation: None of the four evaluated markers associated with glutarate degradation are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize glutarate, as alternative pathways or divergent enzymes may occur.
References: KEGG M00957; KEGG ko00310; Zhang et al. (2018).

Interpretation: Detection of either the GlpK–GlpD pathway, involving glycerol phosphorylation to sn-glycerol-3-phosphate followed by oxidation to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, or the alternative GldA–DhaKLM pathway, involving glycerol oxidation to dihydroxyacetone followed by PEP-dependent phosphorylation to dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
References: Poblete-Castro et al. (2020); KEGG K00864; KEGG K00111; KEGG K00005; KEGG K05878–K05881.

Interpretation: Detection of glycerol kinase or glycerol dehydrogenase without the complete downstream enzymatic machinery required for conversion into dihydroxyacetone phosphate, suggesting potential but incompletely supported glycerol utilization.
References: Poblete-Castro et al. (2020); González et al. (2008).

Interpretation: Detection of isolated enzymes associated with glycerol-3-phosphate metabolism or individual components of the glycerol-processing pathways, without evidence for the initial conversion of free glycerol.
References: KEGG K00057; KEGG K00111–K00113; KEGG K05878–K05881; Poblete-Castro et al. (2020).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with glycerol uptake or metabolism are detected. This does not demonstrate biological inability to utilize glycerol, as alternative pathways or divergent enzymes may occur.
References: KEGG; Poblete-Castro et al. (2020).

Interpretation: Complete glycine cleavage system (GCS), including the P, T, H and L components. The L protein may be shared with other enzyme complexes but is included because it is required for the complete GCS reaction.
References: KEGG M00621; Kikuchi et al. (2008).

Interpretation: Glycine oxidation by glycine oxidase (ThiO), or detection of three of the four GCS components, suggesting a potentially incomplete glycine cleavage system.
References: KEGG K03153; KEGG M00621; Kikuchi et al. (2008).

Interpretation: Isolated GCS components or enzymes associated with glycine and serine metabolism, without sufficient evidence for a complete catabolic pathway.
References: KEGG map00260; Andreesen (1994).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not demonstrate an inability to utilize glycine.
References: KEGG M00621; KEGG map00260.

Interpretation: Complete lactose/L-arabinose ABC transporter coupled to a conventional β-galactosidase or the evolved Ebg enzyme, or a complete lactose-specific PTS coupled to 6-phospho-β-galactosidase.
References: KEGG M00199; KEGG ko00052; Aleksandrzak-Piekarczyk et al. (2005); Solopova et al. (2012).

Interpretation: Partial ABC transporter associated with a lactose-hydrolysing enzyme, partial lactose-specific PTS associated with 6-phospho-β-galactosidase, or complete transport systems lacking the corresponding hydrolytic enzyme. An incomplete Ebg enzyme is also included.
References: KEGG ko00052; Aleksandrzak-Piekarczyk et al. (2005); Solopova et al. (2012); Neves et al. (2005).

Interpretation: Isolated transport components or individual β-galactosidase-related enzymes, including incomplete Ebg subunits, without sufficient evidence for a functional lactose uptake and hydrolysis system.
References: KEGG ko00052; KEGG Orthology; Aleksandrzak-Piekarczyk et al. (2005).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not rule out alternative lactose transport or degradation systems.
References: KEGG M00199; KEGG ko00052.

Interpretation: Direct L-alanine oxidation by alanine dehydrogenase, or the complete Dad pathway involving L- to D-alanine racemization followed by oxidative deamination by D-amino acid dehydrogenase.
References: Reitzer (2005); KEGG R00396; KEGG K00259; KEGG K19244.

Interpretation: Detection of either alanine racemase or D-amino acid dehydrogenase alone, suggesting partial representation of the alternative Dad pathway, without evidence of direct L-alanine dehydrogenase activity.
References: Reitzer (2005); KEGG K01775; KEGG K00285.

Interpretation: Presence of alanine transaminase, an enzyme associated with alanine–pyruvate interconversion, but without sufficient evidence for the catabolism of exogenous L-alanine.
References: Reitzer (2005); KEGG R00258.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not rule out alternative L-alanine utilization pathways.
References: Reitzer (2005); KEGG map00250.

Interpretation: Complete canonical AraA–AraB–AraD pathway, converting L-arabinose into D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which enters the pentose phosphate pathway.
References: KEGG eco00040; Kumar et al. (2024).

Interpretation: Detection of two of the three canonical pathway enzymes, suggesting partial representation of the L-arabinose catabolic pathway.
References: KEGG eco00040; IUBMB EC 5.3.1.4; Kumar et al. (2024).

Interpretation: Isolated canonical pathway enzymes, L-arabinose transport components, or enzymes associated with alternative oxidative or reductive pentose pathways, without sufficient evidence for a complete L-arabinose catabolic route.
References: KEGG Orthology/BRITE; Kumar et al. (2024).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not demonstrate an inability to utilize L-arabinose through alternative pathways.
References: KEGG ko00040.

Interpretation: Complete ADI pathway, arginase-dependent pathway leading to glutamate, or complete arginine succinyltransferase (AST) pathway.
References: Nüse et al. (2023); Hernández et al. (2021); KEGG K01478, K00926.

Interpretation: Partial ADI or AST pathway, partial arginase-dependent degradation, or a combination of arginine decarboxylase and downstream agmatine-processing enzymes.
References: Nüse et al. (2023); Hernández et al. (2021); KEGG map00330.

Interpretation: Isolated enzymes associated with arginine catabolism, agmatine metabolism, or incomplete ADI, arginase-dependent, and AST pathways, without sufficient evidence for a complete catabolic route.
References: Nüse et al. (2023); Hernández et al. (2021); KEGG map00330.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not demonstrate an inability to utilize L-arginine through alternative pathways.
References: KEGG map00330; Nüse et al. (2023).

Interpretation: Presence of L-asparaginase and aspartate ammonia-lyase, supporting the sequential conversion of L-asparagine into L-aspartate and subsequently fumarate, with the release of ammonium.
References: Toyoda et al. (2022); Fisher and Wray (2002); IUBMB EC 3.5.1.1.

Interpretation: Detection of L-asparaginase without the downstream aspartase, or presence of the alternative L-asparaginase-related enzyme K13051, suggesting potential L-asparagine hydrolysis but insufficient evidence for the complete catabolic pathway.
References: Toyoda et al. (2022); KEGG K01424; KEGG K13051.

Interpretation: Presence of L-asparagine transport capacity or aspartate aminotransferases, without evidence of L-asparaginase-mediated hydrolysis.
References: Toyoda et al. (2022); Schubert and Unden (2022); KEGG K11738.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not demonstrate an inability to utilize L-asparagine through alternative pathways.
References: KEGG map00250; Toyoda et al. (2022).

Interpretation: At least one glutamate dehydrogenase and a complete glutamate/aspartate or glutamate-specific ABC transport system are detected, supporting potential substrate uptake and oxidative deamination.
References: KEGG BRITE; KEGG M00233; Straková et al. (2024).

Interpretation: Glutamate dehydrogenase is detected, but neither of the evaluated ABC transport systems is complete. Alternative glutamate uptake systems may be present.
References: KEGG BRITE; Straková et al. (2024).

Interpretation: A complete glutamate/aspartate or glutamate-specific ABC transport system is detected, but no glutamate dehydrogenase is identified.
References: KEGG M00233; Straková et al. (2024).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated glutamate dehydrogenases or ABC transport components were detected. This does not exclude alternative glutamate uptake or catabolic pathways.
References: KEGG BRITE; KEGG M00233.

Interpretation: Complete central Hut pathway, including histidine degradation to formiminoglutamate (FIGLU), together with at least one alternative route for converting FIGLU into L-glutamate.
References: KEGG M00045; Bender (2012).

Interpretation: Detection of two of the three central Hut pathway enzymes, or all three central enzymes without an identified terminal pathway for FIGLU conversion.
References: KEGG M00045; Bender (2012).

Interpretation: Isolated Hut pathway enzymes, terminal FIGLU-processing enzymes, histidine transport components, or histidine decarboxylation markers, without sufficient evidence for a complete histidine catabolic pathway.
References: Bender (2012); KEGG M00045; KEGG BRITE.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not demonstrate an inability to utilize L-histidine through alternative pathways.
References: KEGG M00045; KEGG map00340.

Interpretation: L-lactate uptake through LldP, together with a respiratory L-lactate dehydrogenase (LldD or cytochrome-dependent enzyme) or an alternative lactate 2-monooxygenase.
References: KEGG K29125; KEGG K00101; KEGG K00467; McEwan et al. (2025); Giegel et al. (1990).

Interpretation: Detection of an L-lactate-oxidizing enzyme without the evaluated L-lactate permease. Alternative uptake systems may be present.
References: McEwan et al. (2025); Giegel et al. (1990); KEGG.

Interpretation: Presence of an NAD-dependent L-lactate dehydrogenase, lactate racemase, or L-lactate permease, without sufficient evidence for oxidative L-lactate catabolism.
References: McEwan et al. (2025); KEGG; IUBMB EC 5.1.2.1.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not exclude alternative lactate transport or oxidation pathways.
References: KEGG; McEwan et al. (2025).

Interpretation: Complete reconstruction of at least one of the three bacterial L-lysine degradation pathways: the 5-aminovalerate/glutarate pathway, the cadaverine pathway, or the D-lysine pathway.
References: KEGG M00956; KEGG M00957; KEGG M00960; Revelles et al. (2005); Fothergill and Guest (1977).

Interpretation: Partial reconstruction of one of the bacterial L-lysine degradation pathways, with multiple consecutive pathway steps detected but without sufficient evidence for a complete route.
References: KEGG M00956; KEGG M00957; KEGG M00960; Revelles et al. (2005); Fothergill and Guest (1977).

Interpretation: Detection of isolated markers associated with L-lysine degradation through the cadaverine, 5-aminovalerate/glutarate, D-lysine, pipecolate, or aminoadipate pathways, without sufficient evidence for pathway reconstruction.
References: KEGG M00956; KEGG M00957; KEGG M00960; Revelles et al. (2005); Fothergill and Guest (1977).

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers were detected. This does not exclude alternative L-lysine degradation pathways or uncharacterized enzymes.
References: KEGG ko00310; KEGG M00956; KEGG M00957; KEGG M00960.

Interpretation: Complete reconstruction of the L-proline degradation pathway through either bifunctional PutA or the two independent enzymes, converting L-proline into L-glutamate.
References: KEGG M00970; Moses et al. (2012); Singh & Tanner (2012).

Interpretation: Detection of one of the two independent enzymatic steps, without evidence of the complete catabolic pathway or bifunctional PutA.
References: KEGG M00970; Moses et al. (2012).

Interpretation: Detection of markers associated with proline transport, racemization, or peptide-derived proline release, without sufficient evidence of the complete L-proline catabolic pathway.
References: Moses et al. (2012); KEGG M00970.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated catabolic or related markers were detected.
References: KEGG M00970.

Interpretation: Complete reconstruction of the classical phosphorylative L-rhamnose catabolic pathway, involving RhaA, RhaB and RhaD.
References: KEGG: K01813, K01820, K00848, K01629; Rodionova et al., 2013

Interpretation: Presence of two of the three enzymatic steps of the classical phosphorylative pathway, with the corresponding marker for the third step absent.
References: KEGG: K01813, K01820, K00848, K01629; Boulanger et al., 2021

Interpretation: Presence of a single enzymatic step of the classical pathway or the transport marker K10562, without sufficient evidence to reconstruct the catabolic pathway.
Absence of the evaluated enzymatic and transport markers. This does not exclude the existence of alternative L-rhamnose utilization pathways.
Direct deamination of L-serine to pyruvate and ammonia, catalysed by L-serine dehydratase (SdaA, SdaB or TdcG).
References: KEGG K01752; Reitzer, 2005; BiGG SERD_L

Interpretation: Evidence of L-serine transamination to hydroxypyruvate. The subsequent conversion of hydroxypyruvate to glycerate and its integration into central metabolism are not confirmed by the evaluated markers.
References: KEGG K00830; KEGG K13290; KEGG R00585; Reitzer, 2005

Interpretation: Presence of D-serine dehydratase as the only evaluated serine catabolic marker. This does not provide evidence of L-serine utilization.
References: KEGG K01753.

Interpretation: Absence of the evaluated enzymatic markers.
References: KEGG K01752; KEGG K01753; KEGG K00830; KEGG K13290

Interpretation: Direct degradation of L-tryptophan by tryptophanase, or complete reconstruction of the aerobic kynurenine pathway to anthranilate, followed by its conversion to catechol.
References: KEGG K01667; KEGG M00637; KEGG K00453, K00463, K07130, K01432, K14263, K00486; Kurnasov et al., 2003; Roager & Licht, 2018

Interpretation: Presence of two of the three main enzymatic steps of the aerobic kynurenine pathway, or complete conversion of L-tryptophan to anthranilate without evidence of its subsequent degradation to catechol.
Presence of isolated markers from the kynurenine, anthranilate degradation or alternative tryptophan catabolic pathways, without sufficient evidence to reconstruct a complete degradation route.
References: KEGG KOs; KEGG M00637; Roager & Licht, 2018; Kurnasov et al., 2003

Interpretation: Absence of the evaluated enzymatic markers. This does not exclude the existence of alternative L-tryptophan utilization pathways.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with sucrose uptake and catabolism is detected. This does not exclude alternative transporters or metabolic routes not represented in the analysis.

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with trehalose transport or metabolism is detected. This does not exclude alternative pathways or enzymes not represented in the analysis.
References: Vanaporn and Titball (2020); Shrestha et al. (2024); Ganesh Muthu et al. (2026)

References: Skinner (1938); Anwar et al. (2016); KEGG K00505 and K00832

Interpretation: The combination of D-xylulose reductase (K05351) and xylulokinase (K00854) supports the oxidation of xylitol to D-xylulose and its subsequent phosphorylation to D-xylulose-5-phosphate, enabling its incorporation into the pentose phosphate pathway.

Interpretation: Isolated markers associated with polyol oxidation or D-xylulose assimilation are detected, but the combination required to support a xylitol utilization pathway is not present. K00854 alone does not demonstrate xylitol utilization.
References: Doten and Mortlock (1985); Chen et al. (2010); KEGG K00008 and K00854

Interpretation: None of the evaluated markers associated with xylitol oxidation and subsequent D-xylulose assimilation is detected. This does not exclude alternative enzymes or transport systems not considered in the analysis.
References: Chen et al. (2010); IUBMB EC 1.1.1.9; KEGG map00040
